a: Simeon Peter
t: Simeon: the Hebrew form of Peter's name
p: Only here and in Acts 15:14 is Peter called by the old Hebrew form of his name, Simeon.
b: Symeōn is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Shimon, the name of Jacob's second son. Most of the New Testament uses the shorter Greek name Simōn. The Hebrew form appears for Peter only here and in James's speech in Jerusalem: "Simeon has told how God first showed his care" (Acts 15:14). "Peter" is the Greek for the nickname Jesus gave him, Kepha, "rock" (John 1:42; Matthew 16:18). Readers draw different conclusions. Some hear the voice of a Jewish believer from Palestine, an unusual detail a later imitator would hardly invent. Others reply that a writer imitating Peter could choose the old form on purpose. Some early manuscripts read "Simon" (see the manuscript note).

a: a slave and apostle of Jesus Christ
p: Doulos is a slave, not a hired servant. Peter claims both the lowest title and the highest one.
b: Doulos means a slave: a person owned by a master, as many people in the Roman world were. Many English Bibles say "servant," which softens it. In the Greek Old Testament the great leaders are the LORD's "slaves" (Moses, Joshua, David), so the word is also a title of honor: to belong to God is the highest standing. Jude opens the same way, "a slave of Jesus Christ" (Jude 1), and James too (James 1:1). 1 Peter has "an apostle" alone (1 Peter 1:1). An apostolos is someone sent with authority, here one of those Jesus himself sent. The master of these slaves is Jesus, called "the Master who bought them" in 2:1.

a: a faith just as precious as ours
p: Isotimos means "equal in value." Whoever "ours" means, the readers' faith counts the same.
b: Isotimos means "of equal value" or "equal in honor." "Received" (lanchanō) is the verb for receiving a share by lot, a gift and not an achievement. Who are "we"? (1) The apostles, who saw Jesus (1:16–18): the readers' faith is no second-class faith, though they never saw him. (2) Jewish believers, so that Gentile readers have the same standing (compare Acts 15:8–11, where Peter says God "made no distinction").

a: our God and Savior, Jesus Christ
t: "Our God and Savior": one person or two?
p: One Greek article covers "God" and "Savior," so most read both titles as names for Jesus Christ.
b: The Greek reads tou theou hēmōn kai sōtēros Iēsou Christou: one article ("the") governs both nouns. In such a phrase the two nouns usually name one person (a pattern called the Granville Sharp rule, after the English writer who described it). 2 Peter uses the same shape four more times, where everyone agrees one person is meant: "our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ" (1:11; 2:20; 3:2; 3:18). So most modern scholars and translations read "our God and Savior, Jesus Christ," calling Jesus God, as in "our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ" (Titus 2:13). The KJV's "of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ" separates the two. A few scholars still prefer that, pointing to 1:2, where God and Jesus are named apart.
orig: τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ σωτῆρος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ

a: Grace to you, and peace: may they be multiplied
p: "Grace to you, and peace: may they be multiplied" opens 1 Peter too. Jude has the same verb.
b: This greeting matches 1 Peter 1:2 word for word in Greek: "Grace to you, and peace: may they be multiplied" (1 Peter 1:2). The verb "be multiplied" goes back to the royal letters in Daniel (Daniel 4:1; Daniel 6:25), and Jude uses it too: "may they be multiplied" (Jude 2). 2 Peter adds a phrase of its own, "in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord." Charis, "grace," is kindness given freely; "peace" carries the Hebrew shalom, wholeness and well-being.

a: in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord
p: Epignōsis, "knowledge," is the letter's key word: knowing God and Jesus, not secret information.
b: 2 Peter uses epignōsis four times (1:2, 3, 8; 2:20), the related verb twice (2:21), and the simpler gnōsis three times (1:5, 6; 3:18). The prefix epi- often makes the word stronger, "full knowledge," and in this letter it is the knowledge a person gains in coming to faith: knowing God and Jesus as Lord. If the false teachers claimed a higher knowledge, 2 Peter answers that real knowledge is the knowledge of Christ, and it shows itself in a changed life (1:5–8). The letter ends where it began: "grow ... in the knowledge of our Lord and Savior" (3:18).
orig: ἐν ἐπιγνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν

a: His divine power
p: "Divine power," "divine nature," "godliness," "goodness": 2 Peter speaks the language of Greek religion and ethics.
b: Theios, "divine," appears in the New Testament only here, in 1:4, and in Paul's speech in Athens (Acts 17:29). Eusebeia, "godliness" (reverence for God lived out), and aretē, "goodness" or "excellence," were standard words of Greek moral writing and of public inscriptions praising rulers and benefactors. 2 Peter takes up this vocabulary to say that what Greek thinkers prized as the goal of a good life comes as a gift from Christ. "Called us with his own glory and goodness" may mean that Christ's glory, seen on the mountain (1:16–17), drew the apostles to him.
orig: τῆς θείας δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ (tēs theias dynameōs autou)

a: sharers in the divine nature
p: The boldest phrase in the New Testament about salvation. It is the main text for theosis, or deification.
b: Theias koinōnoi physeōs: "sharers (partners) of divine nature." Greek philosophers spoke of the soul's kinship with the divine, so Greek readers knew the language. 2 Peter places it inside the gospel: it happens "through" God's promises, and it means escape from the "decay" of the world. How far does the phrase go? (1) Theosis: believers truly share God's life by grace, without becoming God by nature. Athanasius wrote, "He was made man that we might be made God" (On the Incarnation 54), and Orthodox teaching builds on this verse: Vladimir Lossky wrote that "in deification we are by grace (that is to say, in the divine energies) all that God is by nature," without our being changed into God's essence. (2) Sharing God's qualities: Calvin wrote that "nature is not here essence but quality." (3) Sharing immortality: escape from decay, as the next words say. See the card on this chapter.
r: John 1:12; John 17:21–23; 2 Corinthians 3:18; 1 John 3:2; Psalms 82:6; John 10:34

a: the world's decay, which comes through desire
p: Phthora is rot and perishing. Desire is the doorway through which it gets in.
b: Phthora means decay, perishing, the opposite of the incorruption that belongs to God (Romans 1:23; 1 Corinthians 15:42). In 2 Peter it is both physical and moral: the false teachers are "slaves of decay" (2:19), and they will be destroyed like animals "born to be trapped and destroyed" (2:12, where the same word is translated "destroyed"). "Desire" (epithymia) is craving that has no limit, the same word used of the teachers' "cravings of the flesh" (2:10, 18) and of the mockers' "own desires" (3:3). The two halves of the verse are opposites: sharing God's nature, or sharing the world's decay.
orig: τῆς ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ φθορᾶς

a: in your faith supply goodness
p: Faith at the start, love at the end: each quality grows inside the one before it.
b: Verses 5–7 form a ladder (in Greek rhetoric, a sorites or "heap"): each new step repeats the last word of the one before. Similar chains appear in Romans 5:3–5 and James 1:3–4. The verb epichorēgeō, "supply," comes from the chorēgos, a wealthy citizen who paid for a city's chorus at the festivals, often generously. So: fund your faith with goodness. The list itself is mostly Greek ethical vocabulary (goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness), framed by two Christian words, faith and love. The same verb returns in 1:11: God will "supply" the way in to the kingdom.
orig: ἐπιχορηγήσατε ἐν τῇ πίστει ὑμῶν τὴν ἀρετήν

a: self-control
p: Enkrateia is mastery over one's appetites. It answers teachers ruled by their cravings.
b: Enkrateia was a favorite virtue of Greek philosophers: the power to rule your own appetites, especially for food, drink and sex. Paul lists it as part of the Spirit's fruit (Galatians 5:23). Its place here is pointed: the false teachers are ruled by "the cravings of the flesh" (2:18) and promise freedom while being slaves (2:19). Hypomonē, "endurance," is staying power under pressure, and it fits readers who are tempted to give up waiting for the Lord's coming (3:4, 9).

a: brotherly love, and in brotherly love, love
p: Philadelphia is love inside the family of believers. Agapē, at the top of the ladder, reaches further.
b: Philadelphia was the word for the affection between brothers and sisters. Christians used it for the family of faith (Romans 12:10; 1 Thessalonians 4:9; 1 Peter 1:22). The last step, agapē, "love," is the widest: the love God shows, which reaches even enemies (Matthew 5:44). Many interpreters see the order as deliberate: faith is the root and love is the crown, as in Paul's "faith, hope, love" (1 Corinthians 13:13).

a: He squints and sees only what is near
p: Myōpazō is to squint, like a nearsighted person. The rare word gives us "myopia."
b: Myōpazō, found only here in the Bible, means to screw up one's eyes, to be nearsighted (the source of "myopia"). How can someone be blind and nearsighted at once? Either the second word explains the first ("blind, that is, shortsighted"), or it says how the blindness came about: by shutting one's eyes to what is far off. That fits the letter well. The person without these qualities sees only the present world and has stopped looking ahead to the Lord's coming (3:4, 12). He has also "forgotten" the cleansing of his sins, while 2 Peter is a letter of reminding (1:12–15; 3:1–2).

a: his old sins were cleansed
p: Most think of baptism, the moment when a believer's past sins were washed away.
b: Katharismos, "cleansing," is the word for ritual purifying in the Greek Old Testament and for Jesus' cleansing of sins (Hebrews 1:3). Many commentators think 2 Peter means baptism, when a believer's former sins were forgiven (Acts 2:38; Acts 22:16; 1 Corinthians 6:11). 1 Peter also connects baptism and a clean conscience (1 Peter 3:21). To forget that cleansing is to live as if it never happened. Compare the warning about those who go back to the mud after being washed (2:22).
r: Hebrews 1:3; Acts 2:38; Acts 22:16; 1 Corinthians 6:11; Ephesians 5:26; 1 Peter 3:21; 2:22

a: brothers
p: The only time 2 Peter says "brothers." The plural includes the women of the church.
b: Adelphoi literally means "brothers," but in Greek the masculine plural covers a mixed group, so the word includes sisters. Elsewhere 2 Peter calls the readers "beloved" (3:1, 8, 14, 17). The site keeps "brothers" in the text, as in Romans and Acts, with the gloss beside it. Calling the church a family was a way of saying that believers belong to one another as kin.

a: make your calling and election firm
p: Not that you can earn God's choice, but that you can make it plain and secure by how you live.
b: Bebaios means firm, secure, legally confirmed. "Calling" and "election" are God's acts: he called them (1:3) and chose them. How can humans make God's choice firm? (1) Assurance: a godly life is the evidence that the calling is real, so believers can be sure of it; good works confirm election to us, not to God. (2) Perseverance as a real condition: the qualities of 1:5–7 are the road on which God's calling reaches its goal, and those who drop them can fall. Calvin took the first: a holy life is "the evidence and proof of election," a sign of it and not its cause. Wesley wrote in the second sense: "If ye are thus diligent to make your election firm, ye shall never finally fall." Both agree on the next line: "you will never trip." The verb (ptaiō) shares its root with Jude's praise of the God who can "guard you from tripping" (Jude 24).
orig: βεβαίαν ὑμῶν τὴν κλῆσιν καὶ ἐκλογὴν ποιεῖσθαι

a: a way in to the eternal kingdom
t: A rich welcome into the kingdom
p: Eisodos is an entrance. The kingdom here is "of our Lord and Savior," Christ's own kingdom.
b: Eisodos means an entrance, a way in, and was also used for a public welcome. "Supplied richly" picks up the verb of 1:5: you supply goodness in your faith, and God will supply the entrance, generously. Only here does the New Testament speak of "the eternal kingdom" of Jesus in these words. Most of the New Testament speaks of "the kingdom of God"; Christ's kingdom appears in Colossians 1:13 and 2 Timothy 4:18. The phrase "our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ" is a favorite of this letter (2:20; 3:2; 3:18).
orig: ἡ εἴσοδος εἰς τὴν αἰώνιον βασιλείαν

a: I will be sure to keep reminding you
p: 1:12–15 is the core of a "testament": a famous person's last words, written down for those left behind.
b: Jewish and Greek readers knew the form of a farewell speech: a leader near death gathers his people, recalls the past, warns about the future and urges them to remember. Jacob (Genesis 49), Moses (Deuteronomy 31–34), Joshua (Joshua 23–24), Paul at Miletus (Acts 20:17–38) and Jesus at the Last Supper (John 13–17) all give such speeches. A whole book, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, gives the deathbed testaments of Jacob's twelve sons. 2 Peter has the marks of the form: the speaker's death is near (1:14), he wants them to remember after he is gone (1:15), and he predicts false teachers (2:1–3; 3:3). Scholars disagree on whether this means Peter wrote his own testament, or a later writer used the form in Peter's name (see the book's opening pages).
r: Genesis 49; Deuteronomy 31:24–29; Joshua 23–24; Acts 20:17–38; John 13–17; 2 Timothy 4:6–8

a: in this tent
p: Skēnōma is a tent. Like a tent, the body is a temporary home that will one day be taken down.
b: Skēnōma is a tent or dwelling. Picturing the body as a tent was common: Paul speaks of the body as an earthly tent (2 Corinthians 5:1–4), and John says the Word "pitched his tent" among us (John 1:14). A tent is the home of a traveler, and 1 Peter calls believers "temporary residents" (1 Peter 1:1). The transfiguration story (1:16–18) has tents too: Peter offered to set up three (Matthew 17:4).
orig: ἐν τούτῳ τῷ σκηνώματι (en toutō tō skēnōmati)

a: just as our Lord Jesus Christ showed me
t: What Jesus showed Peter about his death
p: Probably the word in John 21:18–19 about how Peter would die. The "soon" may also mean "sudden."
b: John 21 records Jesus telling Peter: "when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will tie a belt on you and take you where you do not want to go" (John 21:18), and John adds that this pointed to the death by which Peter would glorify God. Early tradition says Peter died in Rome under Nero, in the mid 60s. Tachinē can mean "soon" or "sudden": either his death is near, or it will come quickly when it comes, as a martyr's death would. Those who doubt that Peter wrote the letter read the verse as the writer's way of placing it on Peter's deathbed; those who accept it read a personal memory. The same word comes back in 2:1, "swift ruin."

a: after my departure
p: Exodos means "departure," a polite word for death, and it is the word used at the transfiguration.
b: Exodos literally means "a way out." It was a gentle way to speak of death (compare Paul's "the time for me to depart is here," 2 Timothy 4:6). It is also the Greek name of the second book of the Bible. And in Luke's account of the transfiguration, Moses and Elijah "were speaking about his exodus, the one he was going to complete in Jerusalem" (Luke 9:31). Since the next verses turn to the transfiguration, the echo may be intended: Peter, like his Lord, has an exodus ahead of him (see the chapter page). "These things" he wants them to recall may be this letter itself, or Peter's teaching as a whole; some readers think of the Gospel of Mark, which early tradition links to Peter.
orig: μετὰ τὴν ἐμὴν ἔξοδον (meta tēn emēn exodon)

a: clever myths that people had invented
p: Mythos meant a story with no factual basis. Someone had said the apostles' message was just that.
b: Mythos could mean any story, but in debates it meant a tale that was not true, such as the stories of the gods that Greek philosophers criticized. Sesophismenos, "made clever," suggests a story crafted to deceive. The Pastoral Letters also warn against "myths" (1 Timothy 1:4; 1 Timothy 4:7; 2 Timothy 4:4; Titus 1:14). The verse sounds like an answer to a charge: someone, perhaps the false teachers, said the promise of Jesus' coming was a fable. 2 Peter answers with eyewitness testimony (see also the note on 3:4).

a: the power and the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ
p: Parousia is "arrival" or "presence," used of a king's official visit. Here it is Jesus' return.
b: Parousia means presence or arrival. In the Greek world it was used of an emperor's or a ruler's state visit to a city, with ceremony and gifts. Christians used it for Jesus' coming at the end (Matthew 24:3; 1 Thessalonians 4:15). "Power and coming" probably means "his coming in power." Some scholars think 2 Peter speaks of his first coming, his life on earth. Most think it means his future return, since the mockers ask, "Where is the promise of his coming?" (3:4), and 3:12 uses the same word. The transfiguration (1:17–18) is then a preview of that glory, as Jesus himself said some would see "the Son of Man coming in his kingdom" (Matthew 16:28).

a: eyewitnesses of his greatness
p: Epoptēs means a spectator. It was also used of people who reached the highest stage of a Greek mystery cult.
b: Epoptēs means an onlooker, someone who watched. In the mystery religions, especially at Eleusis near Athens, the epoptai were initiates who had reached the final stage and seen the holy things. Readers who knew that use might hear a contrast: the apostles truly saw the holy thing. But it was also an everyday word for a watcher (1 Peter 2:12 and 1 Peter 3:2 use the related verb for "seeing"). Megaleiotēs, "greatness, majesty," is used of God's greatness in Luke 9:43.

a: "My Son, my dearly loved one, is this. In him I have found delight."
p: The words differ from all three Gospels, which suggests the writer did not copy any of them.
b: Compare the Gospels: "This is my dearly loved Son; in him I take delight. Listen to him!" (Matthew 17:5); "This is my dearly loved Son. Listen to him!" (Mark 9:7); "This is my Son, the Chosen One. Listen to him!" (Luke 9:35). 2 Peter's form has "my" twice in NA28 and the SBLGNT (once in the Tyndale House GNT; see the manuscript note), puts "this is" last, uses "into whom" (eis hon) rather than "in whom," and has no "Listen to him." The NET Bible's note takes this to mean the writer did not know the Gospels' exact wording. Defenders of Peter as the writer see an eyewitness's own memory; others an oral tradition independent of the written Gospels. The words echo Psalm 2:7 ("You are my son") and Isaiah 42:1 ("He is my chosen one; my soul is pleased with him").
r: Matthew 17:1–8; Mark 9:2–8; Luke 9:28–36; Matthew 3:17; Psalms 2:7; Isaiah 42:1

a: the Majestic Glory
t: The Majestic Glory: a name for God
p: A reverent way of naming God without saying "God," as Jews often did.
b: Megaloprepēs doxa, "the magnificent glory," is a way of referring to God himself, as Jewish speakers often used a reverent title in place of God's name (Matthew 26:64 "the Power"; Hebrews 1:3 "the Majesty on high"). The glory also recalls the bright cloud on the mountain, which in the Old Testament was the sign of God's presence (Exodus 24:15–17; Exodus 40:34).

a: on the holy mountain
p: The Gospels say only "a high mountain." Tradition names Mount Tabor; many scholars prefer Mount Hermon.
b: The Gospels do not name the mountain (Matthew 17:1; Mark 9:2). Christian tradition placed it on Mount Tabor in Galilee. Others point to Mount Hermon, the high mountain near Caesarea Philippi, where the story before it takes place (Mark 8:27). 2 Peter calls it "the holy mountain," a phrase used of Zion in the Psalms (Psalm 2:6): God's presence made it holy, as it made Sinai holy.
r: Matthew 17:1; Mark 9:2; Mark 8:27; Psalms 2:6; Exodus 3:5; Exodus 19:23

a: the prophetic word is all the more firm for us
p: Either the transfiguration confirms the prophets, or the prophets are even surer than the vision.
b: Bebaioteron is a comparative, "firmer," but compared with what? (1) Confirmed by the vision: having seen the glory, we hold the prophetic word as all the more sure. The Plain's "all the more firm for us" follows this reading. (2) Surer than the vision: Scripture is even more reliable than what the apostles saw (the KJV's "a more sure word of prophecy" is often read so). "The prophetic word" may mean the Old Testament prophecies as a whole, a single prophecy such as Psalm 2 or Numbers 24:17, or the whole Old Testament read as prophecy.

a: like a lamp that shines in a murky place
t: A lamp in a murky place
p: Auchmēros means dark and dirty, a dingy, squalid place. The world before the dawn of Christ's coming.
b: Auchmēros means dry, dusty, then dirty and gloomy: a dark, neglected place. The picture is a small lamp in a dingy room through the night. Psalm 119:105 calls God's word a lamp for the feet. The "murky place" is the present world, or the human heart before the day dawns. The lamp is needed only "until" the day comes; prophecy is for the time of waiting.
orig: ὡς λύχνῳ φαίνοντι ἐν αὐχμηρῷ τόπῳ

a: the morning star comes up in your hearts
p: Phōsphoros, "light-bringer," is the morning star, Venus. Jesus calls himself "the bright Morning Star."
b: Phōsphoros, "light-bearer," was the Greek name for the planet Venus as the morning star, which rises just before dawn (the Latin equivalent is Lucifer). Numbers 24:17 promised that "a star" would come out of Jacob, and Jews and Christians read it as a promise of the Messiah. In Revelation Jesus says: "I am the Root and the Descendant of David, the bright Morning Star" (Revelation 22:16). Why "in your hearts"? (1) At his coming Christ will shine in believers' hearts, bringing full understanding. (2) It describes growing inner light now, before his coming. Many commentators take the first, since the "day" is the day of the Lord (3:10).
r: Numbers 24:17; Revelation 22:16; Revelation 2:28; Malachi 4:2; Luke 1:78–79; 2 Corinthians 4:6; 3:10

a: no prophecy of Scripture comes into being by a person's own interpretation
p: The prophet's, or the reader's? Christians have read the verse both ways, and it matters.
b: Idias epilyseōs, literally "of its own untying." Epilysis is explaining, solving a riddle or a dream. (1) The prophet's own interpretation: prophecy did not come from the prophet's own explanation of what he saw. The next verse supports this: "no prophecy was ever borne in by human will." Wesley took it this way: "It is God, not the prophet himself, who thereby interprets." The Plain's "comes into being" takes the verb (ginetai) this way, of where prophecy comes from. (2) The reader's private interpretation: no one may explain prophecy just as he likes (the KJV's "of any private interpretation" is often read so). Catholic teaching sets the reading of Scripture within the Church, while the Reformers taught that "Scripture itself" is the rule of interpretation. See the card on this chapter.

a: people borne along by the Holy Spirit
p: One verb twice: prophecy was not "borne" by human will, but people were "borne along" by the Spirit.
b: The verb pherō appears twice in this verse and twice in 1:17–18 (the voice "carried" from heaven). It can describe a ship driven by the wind (Acts 27:15, 17). The prophets were carried along by the Holy Spirit, and so they "spoke from God." The verse does not explain how much of the prophets' own minds and words remained. Wesley wrote that the prophets "were purely passive therein"; most later theologians stress that God used the writers' own personalities, as their different styles show. With 2 Timothy 3:16 ("Every Scripture is God-breathed and useful") this is a main text for the inspiration of Scripture.
orig: ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίου φερόμενοι (hypo pneumatos hagiou pheromenoi)

a: there were false prophets too
t: False prophets then, false teachers now
p: 2 Peter 2:1–3:3 retells Jude 4–18, starting from Israel's false prophets.
b: From here to 3:3 the letter follows Jude closely (see the topic page Jude and 2 Peter). Jude begins with intruders who "slipped in among you without being noticed" (Jude 4); 2 Peter begins with Israel's history: false prophets once arose "among the people" (the regular term for Israel), as Deuteronomy 13 and 18 and Jeremiah 23 warn. Jesus also warned, "Be on your guard against false prophets" (Matthew 7:15). Notice the shift in tense: the false teachers "will" come (a prediction, as in a farewell speech), but by 2:10–22 the letter speaks of them in the present. They are here already.
r: Jude 4; Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:20–22; Jeremiah 23:9–32; Matthew 7:15; Matthew 24:11; Acts 20:29–30; 1 John 4:1

a: sneak in factions that bring ruin
p: Hairesis meant a school or party. Later it came to mean false teaching: "heresy."
b: Hairesis first meant a choice, then a school of thought or a party: Acts uses it for the "party" of the Sadducees and Pharisees (Acts 5:17; Acts 15:5) and even for the Christians (Acts 24:5). Paul uses it for divisions in the church (1 Corinthians 11:19; Galatians 5:20). Here it begins to take the later sense, "heresy": teaching that splits the church. "Sneak in" (pareisagō) is close to Jude's "slipped in" (pareisdyō), but it is a different verb, so the translation differs. Apōleia, "ruin," is the word of the chapter (2:1 twice, 2:3; 3:7, 16).
r: Acts 5:17; Acts 24:5; 1 Corinthians 11:19; Galatians 5:20; Jude 4; Galatians 2:4

a: disown the Master who bought them
p: Did Christ buy people who end in ruin? The verse is a classic text in the debate over limited atonement.
b: "Master" (despotēs) is the slave owner, and here, as in Jude, the title belongs to Jesus: they "disown our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ" (Jude 4). 2 Peter adds "who bought them": the language of buying a slave at the market (1 Corinthians 6:20; Revelation 5:9). If Christ bought the false teachers, and they go to ruin, then Christ's death was for more than those finally saved. Christ died for all: Wesley drew that conclusion here: "Yet these very men perish everlastingly. Therefore Christ bought even them that perish." Limited ("definite") atonement: John Owen answered that "Master" (despotēs) may mean God the Father, not Christ; that "bought" may mean a deliverance like Israel's from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8; Deuteronomy 15:15), not eternal redemption; and that Peter may speak "according to their apprehension and their profession." Calvin himself read the phrase plainly of Christ, "by whom they have been redeemed," and drew a call to holy living from it. The verse is about their guilt: they disown the owner who paid for them.
r: Jude 4; 1 Corinthians 6:20; 1 Corinthians 7:23; Revelation 5:9; Deuteronomy 7:8; Deuteronomy 15:15; 1 Timothy 2:6; 1 John 2:2

a: Many will follow their shameless self-indulgence
p: Aselgeia, "shameless living," is the same word Jude uses. Here it is plural: their habits of indulgence.
b: Aselgeia is behavior with no restraint, often sexual. Jude says the intruders "turn the grace of our God into shameless self-indulgence" (Jude 4). 2 Peter uses the word three times (2:2, 7, 18) and links it with their promise of "freedom" (2:19). The harm reaches beyond the church: because of them, outsiders will "slander the way of truth." "The way" was an early name for the Christian faith (Acts 9:2; Acts 24:14), and Isaiah 52:5 had already said that God's name is slandered among the nations because of his people (quoted in Romans 2:24).
r: Jude 4; 2:7; 2:18–19; Acts 9:2; Acts 24:14; Isaiah 52:5; Romans 2:24; 1 Timothy 6:1

a: use you to make money
t: Teachers in it for the money
p: Emporeuomai is to trade, to do business. They treat the church as a market.
b: Emporeuomai (our "emporium") means to do business, and with a person as object, to exploit, to sell. "Made-up" (plastos, our "plastic") means shaped, fabricated. Greed (pleonexia, wanting more) is a charge against them again in 2:14, and Balaam, who "loved the pay for wrongdoing" (2:15), is their model. Paying traveling teachers was a live question: Paul defended his right to support but refused it (1 Corinthians 9). Compare Jude: "For pay they have thrown themselves into Balaam's error" (Jude 11).
orig: ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ πλαστοῖς λόγοις ὑμᾶς ἐμπορεύσονται

a: Their ruin is not dozing
p: Their judgment is not idle and their ruin is not dozing: an answer to people who say God's judgment never comes.
b: Two pictures: judgment is a worker who is not idle (argeō), and ruin is a watchman who does not doze (nystazō). Jude said their judgment "was written down long ago" (Jude 4); 2 Peter makes it a judgment set in motion long ago and still active. It sounds like an answer to the claim the letter faces in chapter 3, that God does not judge and everything stays the same (3:4, 9). Compare "the one who guards Israel / does not doze and does not sleep" (Psalm 121:4).
orig: τὸ κρίμα ἔκπαλαι οὐκ ἀργεῖ, καὶ ἡ ἀπώλεια αὐτῶν οὐ νυστάζει

a: threw them into Tartarus
p: Tartarus was the deepest prison of the Greek underworld. 2 Peter uses the Greek word for a Jewish story.
b: Tartaroō, found only here in the Bible, means "throw into Tartarus." In Hesiod's Theogony (about 700 BC) Tartarus is the gloomy pit far below the earth where Zeus bound the rebel Titans. Jewish writers used the word too: 1 Enoch 20:2 sets the archangel Uriel "over the world and over Tartarus." The NET Bible's note says Tartarus was thought of by the Greeks as lower than Hades, a place of divine punishment, and so regarded in Jewish apocalyptic writing too. Verdict: the story is Jewish (Genesis 6 as retold in 1 Enoch; see Jude 6), but 2 Peter tells it with a word Greek readers knew. Many English Bibles say "hell," which blurs it with Gehenna.

a: God did not spare the angels who sinned
p: Jude spoke of angels who left their rank; 2 Peter says only that they "sinned" and drops the details.
b: Jude: "the angels who did not keep to their own rank, but deserted the dwelling that was theirs, he has kept in everlasting chains down in the gloom, for the judgment of the great day" (Jude 6). 2 Peter shortens this. It names no sin except "sinned," leaves out the hint about other flesh, and does not quote 1 Enoch. Perhaps 2 Peter chose not to lean on a book outside Scripture; the letter does not say. Both use "gloom" (zophos) and "kept for judgment." Jude's "chains" are desmois, "bonds"; 2 Peter's word (if "chains" is the right reading; see the manuscript note) is seirais, which Thayer's lexicon gives as "a line, a rope" or "a chain." The Plain says "chains" for both. For which angels are meant (the Watchers of Genesis 6, or a fall before creation), see the note on Jude 6. The sentence that begins here runs, in Greek, all the way to 2:9: "If God did not spare ... then the Lord knows how."

a: Noah, the eighth one
p: Greek "Noah the eighth" means Noah with seven others. 1 Peter 3:20 also counts eight people in the ark.
b: Ogdoon Nōe, "Noah eighth," is a Greek way of saying "Noah and seven others": Noah, his wife, his three sons and their wives (Genesis 7:13). 1 Peter makes the same count: "In it a few, eight souls, were carried safe through water" (1 Peter 3:20). Justin Martyr saw a symbol in the number: the eight in the ark "were a symbol of the eighth day," the day Christ rose from the dead (Dialogue with Trypho 138). The verse adds hopeful examples that Jude does not have: God rescues Noah here and Lot in 2:7. The order also becomes the order of Genesis: angels (Genesis 6), flood (Genesis 7), Sodom (Genesis 19).

a: a herald of righteousness
p: Genesis does not say Noah preached. Jewish tradition did: he warned his generation to repent.
b: Genesis says only that "Noah was a righteous man" (Genesis 6:9). Jewish writers of the time told more. Josephus says Noah, displeased with what the people did, tried to persuade them to change their ways for the better (Antiquities 1.3.1 in Whiston's numbering). The Sibylline Oracles, book 1, give Noah a speech calling the people to repent before the flood. 2 Peter's "herald" (kēryx) is a town crier, a public announcer. Noah fits the letter's scene: a preacher of coming judgment to people who thought life would go on as it always had (3:3–6).

a: reduced the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes
p: Jude says Sodom is "set out as an example" of eternal fire. 2 Peter uses a rare word: turned to ash.
b: Tephroō means "turn to ash." Genesis says "the LORD rained sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah" (Genesis 19:24). Jude: Sodom and Gomorrah "are set out as an example: they suffer the punishment of eternal fire" (Jude 7). 2 Peter also uses "example" (hypodeigma, a model or pattern; Jude's word is deigma) but does not repeat Jude's charge of going "after other flesh." The ruined cities were remembered as a warning all through the Bible (Deuteronomy 29:23; Isaiah 1:9; Amos 4:11; Luke 17:28–30).
r: Genesis 19:24–29; Jude 7; Deuteronomy 29:23; Isaiah 1:9; Amos 4:11; Luke 17:28–30

a: Lot, though, was righteous
p: Genesis shows Lot hesitating and offering his daughters. Jewish tradition and 2 Peter call him righteous.
b: Readers of Genesis 19 may be surprised. Lot lingers when told to leave, and he offers his daughters to the mob. Genesis says he was rescued "because the LORD had pity on him" (Genesis 19:16) and because God "remembered Abraham" (Genesis 19:29). But in Genesis 18:23–32 Abraham pleads for "the righteous" in Sodom, and Lot alone is found. Jewish tradition took that line: the Wisdom of Solomon says Wisdom rescued "the righteous man" who fled the fire on the five cities (Wisdom 10:6). 2 Peter calls Lot "righteous" three times in two verses. The point is not that Lot was perfect, but that he was distressed by evil around him, not part of it, and God knows how to rescue such people.

a: he tortured his own righteous soul
t: Tormented by what he saw and heard
p: Basanizō is to torture. Lot tormented himself, day after day, over what he could not stop seeing.
b: Basanizō is a strong word, used of torture and torment (Matthew 8:29; Revelation 14:10). The active voice suggests Lot tortured his own soul: he could not get used to the evil around him. "Living there among them" (enkatoikeō) is to settle in. Lot had chosen to live near Sodom (Genesis 13:10–13), and he paid for it in distress. The readers, too, live among people whose way of life is "lawless" (athesmos, 2:7; 3:17), and the letter does not tell them to withdraw from the world, but not to be carried away by it.

a: to be punished
t: Punished now, or kept for punishment?
p: The Greek can mean that the wicked are punished already while they wait, or that they are kept for punishment.
b: Kolazomenous is a present participle, "being punished." (1) Punished now: the wicked dead are already under punishment while they wait for the final judgment, as Jesus' story of the rich man in Hades suggests (Luke 16:23). (2) Kept for punishment: the participle points to the future. The Plain's "to be punished" follows this second reading; the Greek itself says only "being punished." The angels of 2:4 are "kept for judgment" in the same way. The verse is the point of the long sentence that began at 2:4: God rescued Noah and Lot and judged the rest, so he can do it again.
orig: ἀδίκους δὲ εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως κολαζομένους τηρεῖν

a: look down on lordship
t: Flesh, lordship and the glorious ones
p: Jude 8 had three charges: stain the flesh, set aside lordship, slander the glorious ones. 2 Peter keeps all three.
b: Compare Jude: "these dreamers, in the same way, stain the flesh, set aside lordship, and slander the glorious ones" (Jude 8). 2 Peter has "go after the flesh" (the phrase Jude 7 uses for Sodom, "went after other flesh"), "look down on" lordship rather than "set aside," and the same "slander the glorious ones." Kyriotēs, "lordship," may be the authority of the Lord, or a rank of angels. Doxai, "glorious ones," are angels, as 2:11 shows. "Daring" (tolmētēs) and "self-willed" (authadēs, pleasing oneself) describe people who fear no one. 2 Peter leaves out Jude's "dreamers" and any hint of visions.
orig: κυριότητος καταφρονοῦντας. Τολμηταί, αὐθάδεις, δόξας οὐ τρέμουσιν

a: do not bring a slanderous judgment
p: Jude told a story about Michael and the devil from a book outside the Bible. 2 Peter speaks only of "angels."
b: Jude: "when Michael the archangel was arguing with the devil, disputing about the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a slanderous judgment against him" (Jude 9). 2 Peter keeps the point and the wording, "bring a slanderous judgment," but drops Michael, Moses and the devil (on that story, see the note on Jude 9). This may be the same reserve as in 2:4. Who are "them"? Probably the evil "glorious ones" of 2:10, fallen angels: even good angels, though stronger, do not insult them, but leave judgment "before the Lord." If the false teachers mock evil powers, they show contempt for a judgment that belongs to God alone.

a: like animals that cannot think
p: Jude 10 compared the teachers to "animals that cannot think." 2 Peter adds the hunt and the slaughter.
b: Jude: "what they grasp by nature, as animals that cannot think do, is what ruins them" (Jude 10). 2 Peter keeps "animals that cannot think" (aloga zōa) and "by nature" (physika, "mere creatures of nature"), and adds that such animals are "born to be trapped and destroyed": wild animals exist, as people thought then, to be hunted. The word phthora is used three times: destruction, destruction, destroyed. The last phrase, "in their destruction," is unclear, and the Plain keeps it as the Greek has it: it may mean that the teachers will be destroyed as the animals are destroyed, or that they will perish in their own corruption, or along with the evil powers they slander.
orig: ὡς ἄλογα ζῷα γεγεννημένα φυσικὰ εἰς ἅλωσιν καὶ φθοράν

a: the pay for the harm they do
p: A play on words: adikoumenoi misthon adikias, "wronged as the wage of wrong."
b: The Greek repeats one root: adikoumenoi, "being wronged," misthon adikias, "the pay of wrongdoing." They will suffer the harm they caused, a judgment that fits the crime. The NET Bible's note says this wordplay is hard to bring into English. "Pay" (misthos) links them to Balaam, "who loved the pay for wrongdoing" (2:15), and to Jude: "For pay they have thrown themselves into Balaam's error" (Jude 11). Some manuscripts read "they will receive the pay" (see the manuscript note).

a: To them, luxury in the daytime is pleasure
p: Feasting began in the evening. Drinking by day was the mark of the shameless.
b: In the ancient world respectable people worked by day and dined in the evening. To feast and drink in daylight was a sign of laziness and excess: "Woe to you, land! Your king is a lad, / and your princes eat at daybreak" (Ecclesiastes 10:16). Paul urges believers to walk "in a decent way, as in daylight" (Romans 13:13; compare 1 Thessalonians 5:7). Tryphē is luxury, soft living; hēdonē (our "hedonism") is pleasure, the goal of life according to the Epicureans, or so their critics said.
orig: ἡδονὴν ἡγούμενοι τὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τρυφήν

a: They are stains and flaws
p: Jude called them "sunken rocks" (spilades) at the love feasts. 2 Peter has a near twin: spiloi, "stains."
b: Jude: "These people are sunken rocks at your love feasts" (Jude 12). The Greek spilades means hidden reefs. 2 Peter writes spiloi kai mōmoi, "stains and flaws," two words that describe a sacrificial animal that is not fit for God (compare 1 Peter 1:19, "a lamb with no flaw and no stain"). The same two words, in the same order, return in 3:14 with the sense turned around: believers must be found "without stain and without flaw." Where Jude has "love feasts" (agapais), 2 Peter has "deceptions" (apatais), a word that differs by a couple of letters; some manuscripts of 2 Peter have "love feasts" (see the manuscript note). "As they feast with you" is the same verb as in Jude 12.

a: Their eyes are full of an adulteress
p: Not just "adultery": the Greek is "an adulteress," as if a woman were always in their eyes.
b: Moichalis means an adulteress, so the phrase is vivid: they cannot look at a woman without seeing a possible lover (compare Matthew 5:28). "Never rest from sin" uses a word for something that cannot be stopped. "Bait" (deleazō) is a fishing and hunting word, to lure with bait, used again in 2:18. "Well exercised" (gegymnasmenēn, from the gymnasium) means trained like an athlete: their hearts have had a long workout in greed. "Children of a curse" is a Hebrew way of saying "people under a curse" (compare Ephesians 2:3, "children of wrath").

a: Balaam son of Bosor
t: Balaam son of Bosor, not Beor
p: Numbers calls Balaam "son of Beor." Most Greek editions of 2 Peter have "Bosor." Why?
b: Numbers says Balak sent for "Balaam son of Beor" (Numbers 22:5). Here NA28, the SBLGNT, the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus read Bosor; Thayer's lexicon notes that Westcott and Hort printed Beōr. The NET Bible's note says English versions that print "Beor" here have harmonized with the Old Testament rather than followed a Greek reading. Explanations of "Bosor": (1) Pronunciation: Thayer's Greek lexicon explains it as the Hebrew letter ayin of Beor written with a Greek s. (2) A pun: Hebrew basar means "flesh," so "son of flesh" would fit teachers who "go after the flesh" (2:10). Neither can be proved.
r: Numbers 22:5; Numbers 22–24; Numbers 31:16; Deuteronomy 23:4; Jude 11; Revelation 2:14

a: a voiceless beast of burden, speaking out in a human voice
p: Numbers 22:21–35: the donkey sees the angel, Balaam does not. Here the beast rebukes the prophet.
b: "Then the LORD opened the donkey's mouth, and she said to Balaam, 'What have I done to you, that you have beaten me these three times?'" (Numbers 22:28). In Numbers it is the angel who rebukes Balaam (Numbers 22:32); 2 Peter credits the donkey, which first stopped him. Hypozygion, "beast under the yoke," was a common word for a donkey. Paraphronia, "madness," means being out of one's right mind. The irony is the point: a dumb animal had more sense than a prophet who loved money. Compare the false teachers, "animals that cannot think" (2:12).

a: waterless springs and mists driven by a squall
p: Jude has "waterless clouds swept along by winds." 2 Peter has dry springs and mists blown by a storm.
b: Jude: "They are waterless clouds swept along by winds" (Jude 12), and "wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept forever" (Jude 13). 2 Peter keeps "waterless" but makes it springs: in a dry land a spring that has failed is a cruel disappointment (Jeremiah 2:13; Jeremiah 15:18). The clouds become "mists" (homichlai) driven by a squall (lailaps, a sudden storm), which promise rain and give none. 2 Peter drops Jude's waves and stars and goes straight to the end: "the gloom of darkness has been kept" for them, as for the angels of 2:4.
orig: πηγαὶ ἄνυδροι καὶ ὁμίχλαι ὑπὸ λαίλαπος ἐλαυνόμεναι

a: puffed-up words of emptiness
p: Jude: "Their mouths speak puffed-up words." 2 Peter adds "of emptiness."
b: Jude: "Their mouths speak puffed-up words" (Jude 16). Hyperonka means swollen, inflated; mataiotēs, "emptiness, futility," is the Greek Bible's word for the "vapor" of Ecclesiastes. Their bait is "the cravings of the flesh": they offer people who have only just left a pagan way of life the freedom to go back to it with a clear conscience. Those they target are "truly getting away" (or "barely getting away": see the manuscript note) from "those who spend their lives in error," most likely their old pagan neighbors.

a: They promise them freedom
p: Freedom from moral rules, from fear of judgment, or both. 2 Peter answers: whatever beats you owns you.
b: The teachers' message seems to have been "freedom." Readings: (1) Paul misunderstood: the teachers twisted Paul's message of freedom from the law (Galatians 5:13) into freedom to sin, which Paul himself rejected ("Should we stay in sin so that grace may multiply?", Romans 6:1). 3:15–16 suggests Paul's letters were being twisted. (2) Freedom from fear of judgment: if there is no coming and no judgment (3:4), there is nothing to fear. Many scholars compare the Epicureans, who taught that the gods do not judge, so that people could be free of fear: David deSilva calls freedom "an explicit Epicurean goal," and Peter Davids follows Jerome Neyrey in placing the readers among Gentiles influenced by Epicurean teaching (as Ernst Baasland's review of Davids reports). The answer sounds like a proverb: a person is the slave of whatever defeats him (compare John 8:34; Romans 6:16).
r: Galatians 5:1; Galatians 5:13; Romans 6:1; Romans 6:16; John 8:34; 1 Peter 2:16; 3:4; 3:15–16

a: then in the end they are worse off than at the beginning
p: The words match Jesus' saying about the unclean spirit that comes back with seven others.
b: The Greek ta eschata cheirona tōn prōtōn is the same phrase as in Jesus' saying about the evil spirit that returns to a swept house with seven worse spirits: "In the end that person is worse off than at the beginning" (Matthew 12:45; Luke 11:26). Who are "they"? (1) The false teachers, who once knew Christ and turned away (most commentators). (2) The new believers they lure back (2:18). "Filth" (miasmata) is defilement, the stains of the pagan world. "Tangled up" (emplekō) pictures a net or a snare. For the question whether a true believer can fall away, see the note on 2:21.
orig: γέγονεν αὐτοῖς τὰ ἔσχατα χείρονα τῶν πρώτων

a: the holy command that was handed down to them
t: Can a true believer fall away?
p: These verses are central in the debate over perseverance. The churches read them very differently.
b: "Handed down" is the word Jude uses for "the faith that was handed down to the saints once for all" (Jude 3). People who knew "the way of righteousness" and turned back would have been better off never knowing it. Readings: (1) A real fall: these were real believers who escaped the world "by knowing the Lord and Savior" (2:20) and then fell away. Wesley read the dog and the sow of 2:22 as people "after they have made shipwreck of the faith." (2) Not the fall of true believers: they had knowledge and a cleaned-up life, like the washed pig of 2:22, which never changed its nature. Calvin wrote on this verse that "the faithful also do indeed sin," but "they do not fall away from the grace of God," and John Owen said that the false teachers of 2:1 had "only common gifts of light and knowledge." The same debate surrounds Hebrews 6:4–6 and 10:26–31; the "Where Christians differ" card at Hebrews 6:4–6 sets the churches' answers side by side, and the topic page Can Believers Fall Away? gathers the passages.

a: "A dog turns back to its own vomit,"
t: Two proverbs: the dog and the sow
p: The dog comes from Proverbs 26:11. The washed sow appears in the Story of Ahiqar.
b: The first saying comes from Proverbs: "A dog goes back to its vomit, / and a fool does his folly over again" (Proverbs 26:11). 2 Peter's Greek is not the Septuagint's wording, which suggests a proverb known by heart. The second is not in the Bible. A close parallel stands in the Story of Ahiqar, an ancient Near Eastern tale of a wise man, known in Aramaic, Syriac and Arabic: in the Syriac version, the bad son is like a pig that had been to the baths and then, seeing a muddy ditch, went down and washed in it (Ahiqar 8:18, Syriac, in R. H. Charles's edition). Jews counted dogs and pigs unclean, and both images say the same thing: washing on the outside does not change the nature. Compare Jesus: "Do not toss your pearls down in front of pigs" (Matthew 7:6).

a: I am already writing you this second letter
p: Most think the first letter is 1 Peter. Others think it is a lost letter, or the first two chapters of this one.
b: "Second letter" assumes the readers know a first. (1) 1 Peter, the most common view, which makes the readers the churches of Asia Minor named in 1 Peter 1:1. (2) A lost letter, since 1 Peter says little about the false teachers or the Lord's coming, the themes 3:1–2 says both letters share. (3) Chapters 1–2, if chapter 3 was once a separate letter (few hold this). Scholars who think the letter is pseudonymous often see 3:1 as the writer's way of linking his work to the known letter of Peter. The two letters' Greek styles differ a good deal, which Jerome explained by Peter's use of different interpreters (Letter 120). "Beloved" (agapētoi) is how Jude addresses his readers too (Jude 3, 17, 20).

a: the words spoken beforehand by the holy prophets
p: Jude 17 says, "remember the words spoken beforehand by the apostles." 2 Peter adds the holy prophets.
b: Jude: "you, beloved, must remember the words spoken beforehand by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Jude 17). 2 Peter adds "the holy prophets" and so puts the Old Testament prophets and the apostles side by side, as in Ephesians 2:20 and 3:5. "Your apostles" means the apostles who brought the good news to these readers. The Greek is a bare chain of possessives, "the command of your apostles of the Lord and Savior"; the Plain supplies "passed on from" to make English of it. In the Textus Receptus the KJV reads "us the apostles" (see the manuscript note). The "command" is the way of life taught by Jesus, the same "holy command" of 2:21. Many scholars see the phrase "your apostles," spoken as if from outside the group, as a sign of a later date; others note that Peter could speak of the apostles who founded a church he had not founded.

a: in the last days mockers will come with their mocking
p: Jude 18 quotes the apostles: "In the last time there will be mockers." 2 Peter gives the mockers' words.
b: Jude: "They kept telling you, 'In the last time there will be mockers who live by their own ungodly desires'" (Jude 18). 2 Peter's Greek follows closely and adds "with their mocking," a doubling found in Hebrew style ("mockers in mockery"). 2 Peter goes further than Jude by quoting the mockers (3:4). "The last days" is the prophets' phrase for the time when God acts at last (Isaiah 2:2), which the apostles said had begun with Jesus (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2). Here the parallel with Jude ends.
r: Jude 18; Jude 17; Isaiah 2:2; Acts 2:17; 2 Timothy 3:1–5; 1 Timothy 4:1; Hebrews 1:2

a: Where is the promise of his coming?
p: The mockers' question: Jesus has not come, and nothing has changed since the world began.
b: "Where is ...?" was a mocking question in the Psalms and prophets: "Where is your God?" (Psalm 42:3); "Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come!" (Jeremiah 17:15). The argument has two parts. (1) Delay: the coming was promised soon, and it has not happened. (2) A closed world: everything has always gone on the same since creation, so God does not step in to judge. Scholars compare Epicurean philosophy, which taught that the gods do not intervene in the world, and that fear of judgment after death is groundless; David deSilva says that the majority of scholars now place the rival teachers against this background; Peter Davids, following Jerome Neyrey, is one of them (as Ernst Baasland's review of Davids reports). Others think the problem was simply the long wait. The letter answers both parts: God has stepped in before (3:5–6), and God's time is not ours (3:8–9).
r: Psalms 42:3; Psalms 79:10; Jeremiah 17:15; Malachi 2:17; Ezekiel 12:22; Matthew 24:48; 3:5–9

a: Since the day the fathers fell asleep
p: Either Israel's ancestors (as nearly everywhere in the Bible) or the first Christian generation, now dead.
b: "The fathers" normally means Israel's patriarchs and ancestors (Romans 9:5; Hebrews 1:1), and some commentators read it so here: since the patriarchs died, nothing has changed. But then the complaint has nothing to do with the delay of Jesus' coming. So many scholars think "the fathers" are the first generation of Christians, who were expected to see the Lord come (compare Mark 9:1; 1 Thessalonians 4:15), and who have now "fallen asleep," the usual Christian picture for death. If so, the letter was written after many of that generation had died, a point in the case for a later date. Defenders of Peter as writer either take the first reading, or note that by the mid 60s many first believers had died.
orig: ἀφ’ ἧς γὰρ οἱ πατέρες ἐκοιμήθησαν
r: Romans 9:5; Hebrews 1:1; Mark 9:1; Matthew 16:28; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–15; John 21:22–23

a: an earth that took shape out of water and by means of water
t: A world made out of water
p: Genesis 1: the waters at the start, and dry ground called out of them by God's word.
b: In Genesis 1 the world begins with water, "God's Spirit fluttered over the face of the waters" (Genesis 1:2), and God makes a dome to divide the waters (Genesis 1:6) and says, "Let the waters under the sky be gathered to one place, and let dry ground be seen" (Genesis 1:9). Everything happens "by the word of God" (compare Psalm 33:6; Hebrews 11:3). The mockers say the world is stable and nothing ever changes. 2 Peter answers that the world has always depended on God's word, and the same water from which the earth was formed was the water that drowned it.
r: Genesis 1:2; Genesis 1:6–10; Psalms 24:2; Psalms 33:6; Hebrews 11:3; Genesis 7:11

a: the world of that day was flooded with water and came to ruin
p: God has already ended one world. The mockers "want" to forget it.
b: "Flooded" (kataklyzō) is the verb behind the noun "flood" (kataklysmos) of 2:5. In Genesis the flood came when "all the springs of the great deep burst open, and the windows of the sky were opened" (Genesis 7:11), so the water from below and the water above, separated at creation, came together again. The world did not cease to exist, but "the world of that day," its order and people, came to ruin. Jesus used the same comparison: people were eating and drinking, and did not know until the flood came (Matthew 24:37–39). "Through these" is plural, and the NET Bible's note finds its reference unclear: the heavens, the heavens and earth, or (most likely, it says) the water and the word of 3:5. NA28 prints a singular, "through which," that would point to the word alone (see the manuscript note).
orig: ὁ τότε κόσμος ὕδατι κατακλυσθεὶς ἀπώλετο

a: have been put in storage for fire
p: Greek Stoics taught that the world would end in fire and be reborn. Jewish writers spoke of judgment by fire.
b: The present heavens and earth are "stored up" (thēsaurizō, put in a treasury) for fire. Many ancient readers had heard of a world-fire. Stoic philosophers taught that the universe goes through endless cycles, each ending in a great blaze (ekpyrōsis), after which all begins again. Jewish texts spoke of judgment by fire: "the LORD will come in fire" (Isaiah 66:15); "the day is coming, burning like an oven" (Malachi 4:1). The Life of Adam and Eve, a Jewish writing, has Eve say God will judge the human race "first by water, the second time by fire" (49:3). Verdict: 2 Peter's picture is Jewish and biblical: one judgment, not an endless cycle; the fire is "for the day of judgment," aimed at "ungodly people." Its readers would still have heard the Stoic echo.

a: in the Lord's sight one day is like a thousand years
t: A thousand years like one day
p: Psalm 90:4 says it to show God's greatness. 2 Peter uses it to answer the charge that God is late.
b: Psalm 90 says: "For a thousand years, as you see them, / are like yesterday after it has gone by" (Psalm 90:4). The psalm sets God's eternity against human shortness of life. 2 Peter adds the reverse, "a thousand years like one day," and applies it to the delay: God does not measure time as we do, so "late" is a human judgment. Jewish writers used the verse to count time too: Jubilees 4:30 says Adam died seventy years short of a thousand, "for one thousand years are as one day in the testimony of the heavens" (in R. H. Charles's translation), so he died within the "day" of Genesis 2:17. Early Christians read the six days of creation as six thousand years of history, after which the Lord would end all things (Barnabas 15; Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.28.3), a reading still behind some millennial counting today. 2 Peter itself does no counting; its point is that God's timing cannot be measured by ours.

a: He does not want any to be lost, but wants all to arrive at repentance
p: One of the Bible's strongest statements that God wants everyone to repent. How "all" is read divides Christians.
b: The delay is not slowness but patience (makrothymeō, to be long-suffering), as Paul says, "God's kindness is leading you to repentance" (Romans 2:4). Compare "He wants everyone to be saved and to arrive at full knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4) and Ezekiel's "Do I not take pleasure when he turns away from his ways and lives?" (Ezekiel 18:23). Readings of "any" and "all": (1) Every human being: Wesley's note says, "Not willing that any soul, which he hath made should perish." Calvin also read it of all people: "So wonderful is his love towards mankind, that he would have them all to be saved"; he explained that the verse speaks of God's will "as made known to us in the gospel," not of "the hidden purpose of God." (2) All of "you," the elect: John Owen held that "us" must be supplied in both clauses, "Not willing that any of us should perish," meaning the beloved, chosen readers; the verse does say he is patient "with you." The NET Bible's note mentions this debate. The card on 1 Timothy 2:4 sets out how the churches answer. "Repentance" (metanoia) means turning your life around.
orig: μὴ βουλόμενός τινας ἀπολέσθαι ἀλλὰ πάντας εἰς μετάνοιαν χωρῆσαι
r: Romans 2:4; 1 Timothy 2:4; Ezekiel 18:23; Ezekiel 33:11; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2

a: like a thief
t: The day of the Lord comes like a thief
p: Jesus' picture of the thief became the church's standard way to speak of the end: it comes without warning.
b: "The day of the Lord" is the prophets' name for the day God comes to judge (Amos 5:18; Joel 2:31; Malachi 4:5). Jesus compared his coming to a burglar (Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39), and the early church kept the image: "the day of the Lord is coming the way a thief comes at night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2); "I will come like a thief" (Revelation 3:3; compare Revelation 16:15). A thief does not announce himself. So the long delay the mockers point to is no proof that the day will not come; the delay is exactly what a thief's coming looks like.
r: Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39; 1 Thessalonians 5:2; Revelation 3:3; Revelation 16:15; Amos 5:18; Joel 2:31

a: the elements will burn and be dissolved
p: Stoicheia: the basic parts of matter, the stars and planets, or the spirit powers. All three have defenders.
b: Stoicheia means the basic parts of a series: letters of the alphabet, then the building blocks of the world. Paul's phrase "the basic elements of the world" (Galatians 4:3) is a different case. Readings here: (1) The physical elements, earth, water, air and fire in Greek thought, the stuff the world is made of; Thayer's lexicon lists these verses under "the elements from which all things have come." (2) The heavenly bodies, sun, moon and stars, which early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr also called stoicheia (so Thayer); this fits Isaiah 34:4, "the sky will roll up like a scroll," and Jesus' words that the stars will fall (Mark 13:25). (3) The spirit powers thought to rule the heavens. The order here, heavens, then elements, then earth, fits (2) well. "Burn" (kausoō) is used for a fever, intense heat.

a: the heavens will go by with a rushing roar
p: Rhoizēdon is the whoosh of something rushing: an arrow, wings, a roaring fire.
b: Rhoizēdon, found only here in the Bible, imitates a rushing sound, like the whir of wings, the hiss of an arrow or the roar of flames. That the heavens "pass away" is said by Jesus too: "Heaven and earth will be gone, but my words will never be gone" (Matthew 24:35). The prophets used such pictures (Isaiah 34:4; Isaiah 51:6), and Revelation sees "a new heaven and a new earth" after "the first heaven and the first earth had gone away" (Revelation 21:1). Whether this means the end of the material universe, or its purging and renewal, is the debate of 3:10–13 (see the chapter page).
r: Matthew 24:35; Isaiah 34:4; Isaiah 51:6; Hebrews 12:26–27; Revelation 6:14; Revelation 21:1

a: the earth and the works in it
t: "Will lie exposed": the Greek says "will be found"
p: The oldest Greek ends the verse with "will be found." The Plain says "will lie exposed" so the English makes sense.
b: The last word of the verse in the oldest Greek copies is heurethēsetai, "will be found." Said of the earth and the works in it, "found" means found out, uncovered, with nothing hidden from God, so the Plain says "will lie exposed." The same verb comes back four verses later: "be eager to be found by him without stain and without flaw" (3:14). On the day when the whole earth is found, the readers are to make sure how they themselves will be found. Al Wolters reads "found" as a metalworkers' word for what is left after the fire, a world purified rather than destroyed; on that reading too, what remains lies open. For the other manuscript readings ("burned up," "will not be found") see the manuscript note, and for the readings of the whole verse see the chapter page.
orig: καὶ γῆ καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ ἔργα εὑρεθήσεται (kai gē kai ta en autē erga heurethēsetai)

a: how holy your ways of life must be
p: The end of the world is not given to satisfy curiosity. It is a reason to live differently now.
b: Potapous asks "what sort of people." The answer is in plurals: "holy ways of life" (hagiais anastrophais) and "acts of godliness" (eusebeiais), many daily acts rather than one feeling. This is the letter's ethics in one sentence: since all these things are being dissolved, what lasts is how you live before God. The same move is made by Jesus (Matthew 24:42–46), Paul (Romans 13:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 5:4–8) and 1 Peter ("The end of all things has come close. So be sensible and keep a clear head for prayer," 1 Peter 4:7).
orig: ποταποὺς δεῖ ὑπάρχειν ὑμᾶς ἐν ἁγίαις ἀναστροφαῖς καὶ εὐσεβείαις

a: hurry it along
p: Can believers make the end come sooner? 2 Peter seems to say so: by repentance and holy living.
b: Speudō can mean "be eager for" or "hasten." Most commentators take "hasten": believers can speed up the day of God. How? By holy lives, prayer ("May your kingdom come," Matthew 6:10) and the repentance God is waiting for (3:9). Compare Peter's sermon in Acts: "So repent and turn around, to have your sins wiped away. Then times of relief may come from the Lord's presence" (Acts 3:19). The verse balances 3:9: God waits for repentance, and believers can hurry the day by living it. "The day of God" is a rare phrase (Revelation 16:14).

a: new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness makes its home
t: New heavens and a new earth
p: The promise of Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. Righteousness, which is a stranger now, will settle there for good.
b: "For look, I am creating new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17), and "the new heavens and the new earth / that I am making will stand before me" (Isaiah 66:22). Revelation 21:1 sees it: "Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth." Kainos, "new," can mean new in quality, renewed, not only brand new. "Makes its home" (katoikeō) is to settle permanently. In the present world the righteous are like Lot in Sodom (2:7–8); in the new one, righteousness itself will be at home. "His promise" answers the mockers' "Where is the promise?" (3:4).
orig: καινοὺς δὲ οὐρανοὺς καὶ γῆν καινήν

a: to be found by him without stain and without flaw
p: "Found" again, as in 3:10, and the opposite of the teachers, who are "stains and flaws" (2:13).
b: Two links tie this verse to the rest of the letter. "Be found" picks up 3:10, where the Greek says the earth and its works "will be found" (the Plain: "will lie exposed"): may you be found clean. "Without stain and without flaw" (aspiloi kai amōmētoi) turns around the words used of the false teachers, "stains and flaws" (spiloi kai mōmoi, 2:13). The words describe an animal fit for sacrifice, and Christ himself, "a lamb with no flaw and no stain" (1 Peter 1:19). "In peace" may mean at peace with God, or at peace with one another, against the factions of 2:1.
orig: ἄσπιλοι καὶ ἀμώμητοι αὐτῷ εὑρεθῆναι ἐν εἰρήνῃ

a: Our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you this way
p: Warm words about Paul, whom Peter had once clashed with in Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14).
b: "Our beloved brother Paul" shows the two apostles as partners. Galatians 2:11–14 tells of Paul's open rebuke of Peter at Antioch. Readings: (1) Peter's own reconciliation: if Peter wrote this near his death, the quarrel at Antioch lay years behind him, and he warmly endorses Paul. (2) A later voice: many scholars think a later writer, in Peter's name, presents the two apostles in harmony at a time when Paul's letters were being claimed by false teachers. What did Paul write "to you" about God's patience? Perhaps Romans 2:4 ("God's kindness is leading you to repentance"), or letters to the churches of Asia Minor such as Galatians, Ephesians or Colossians. "The wisdom that was given to him" is a humble way of saying that Paul's insight came from God (1 Corinthians 3:10).
r: Galatians 2:7–14; Romans 2:4; Romans 9:22; 1 Corinthians 3:10; Acts 15:7–11; 1 Peter 5:12

a: the other Scriptures
p: "The other Scriptures" puts Paul's letters alongside the Scriptures. It is a key verse for the history of the canon.
b: Tas loipas graphas, "the other (rest of the) Scriptures," treats Paul's letters as Scripture. The NET Bible's note says this one incidental line links Paul's writings with Scripture. Two questions follow. (1) The canon: this is the only place where a New Testament letter explicitly puts Paul's letters with "the other Scriptures." (1 Timothy 5:18 may also call a saying of Jesus "Scripture"; which came first depends on how each letter is dated.) (2) The date: "all his letters" sounds like a known collection of Paul's letters. Many scholars think such a collection, read in churches alongside the Old Testament, points to a date after Paul's death, perhaps late in the first century. Others answer that Paul's letters were copied and shared while he lived (Colossians 4:16), and that an apostle could recognize another apostle's writing as from God. "Hard to grasp" is a frank admission that Christians have shared ever since. Dei Verbum 11 cites this passage, with 2 Peter 1:19–20, for the teaching that Scripture is written under the Holy Spirit.
orig: ὡς καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς γραφάς (hōs kai tas loipas graphas)

a: Ignorant and unsteady people will twist these
p: Streblōo is to twist on the rack. The "unsteady" are the same people the false teachers "bait" in 2:14.
b: Strebloō means to twist or wrench, as on a torturer's rack. The twisters are "ignorant" (amatheis, untaught) and "unsteady" (astēriktoi), the same word as the "unsteady souls" of 2:14, while the readers "stand firm" (1:12) and must not lose their "firm footing" (3:17): all from one Greek root (stērizō). Which parts of Paul were being twisted? Most likely his teaching on grace and freedom (see 2:19; Romans 3:8, where Paul complains of people saying he taught "Let us do evil so that good may come"), or on the timing of the end (2 Thessalonians 2:1–2). NA28 prints the future, "will twist," as a prediction; other editions have the present (see the manuscript note).

a: keep growing in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ
p: The letter ends where it began, with knowledge of Christ, and turns the warning into a command to grow.
b: "Grow" is the opposite of "fall" (3:17). The letter opened with grace and "the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord" (1:2) and a ladder of growth (1:5–8); it closes with grace and knowledge again. The doxology gives glory to Jesus, which in Jewish practice belonged to God alone (compare Romans 16:27; Jude 25, where glory goes to God "through Jesus Christ"). "The day of eternity" (hēmera aiōnos), found only here, may mean "forever," or the day of the Lord that opens the eternal age: the day the whole letter has been looking toward.
orig: αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς ἡμέραν αἰῶνος
